game:item-handbooktext-boat-sailed-*:
Sailboats are constructed in place on land, and then rolled into the water. They cannot be picked up. They can be deconstructed by holding down rightmouse with a saw. See the Building A Sailboat entry for more information.

Movement
Once you have constructed your sailboat, rightmouse click on the starboard aft seat (by the tiller at the stern) to sit in that seat: only that seat can control the boat. With the sails furled, you can use normal navigation keys to move the boat slowly. rightmouse-click on the cleat on the side of the mast (where a rope is tied) to unfurl the sail and pick up speed. The sailboat currently does not respond to wind direction, only your movement keys.

If the boat becomes grounded or in water that is too shallow, it can be moved very slowly using the arrow keys, but only with the sail furled again.

Equipping
Most boat accessories are added to the boat via ctrl + rightmouse.
The boat can also hold several passengers - in every boat, one passenger can sit on the port-side aft seat (adjacent to the player who is at the tiller controlling the boat). Additional seats can be added to any of the eight cargo hold spots.

You can place containers (including chests, baskets, and storage vessels) in the hold of the boat, and access them on or off the boat.

You can also place a mount (such as an elk) on the boat by first placing a wooden fence post in one of the cargo spots - being sure to leave 2 cargo spots empty aft of the post - and then using a rope on this fence post, which will place the animal into the aft cargo spots. You can then disembark the animal using rightmouse on the fence post.

You can attach a lantern to the aft face of the mast (about 3 meters up) to provide light.

Ratlines can be attached to the gunwhales on each side of the mast in order to allow you to climb to the top of the mast to look around.

An anchor can be placed in the front-left space in the prow. With an empty hand, rightmouse click it to let it go or haul it up; see Mooring and Anchoring.

There is also a spot at the prow for a figurehead to be placed (you can also place your own chiseled figurehead there), and on the port bow, your boat can be named (using pigment and shift + rightmouse-click).
game:item-handbooktext-anchor-stone: The stone anchor can be placed in the front-left prow location of the sailboat (and only this spot). With an empty hand, rightmouse click it to let it go or haul it up. It holds when about five times the depth of the water in rope is let out; see Mooring and Anchoring.
vessel-grease-in: Grease due in {p0:less than a day|# day|# days}
vessel-nothing-to-grease: The hull is well greased: nothing to grease yet
vessel-nothing-to-mend: The hull is sound: nothing to mend
itemdesc-anchorwarp: Nine ropes spliced into 90 metres of warp. Stowed at a sailboat's mast, it lets the anchor reach deeper water.
itemdesc-bark-birch: Peeled from a birch log with a knife. It builds a birch-bark canoe, and mends one on the way.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:re:
A one-way crossing: quick to bind from reeds with a knife, light to carry, and it soaks up water and falls apart within about three days afloat. It cannot be mended. It carries one person and a basket.
- Place it with a rightmouse click and paddle it with an oar.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:du:
One log hollowed out: the toughest hull before planks, barely scratched by rocks, and it needs no upkeep. Too heavy to carry; a workhorse of rivers and lakes. Tippy in a sea: it rolls hard and ships water over its low sides; bail it with a bowl, jug or bucket before it swamps.
- Place it with a rightmouse click where it will stay, and paddle it with an oar.
- Mend it with a log of its wood.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:co:
A round bowl of hide for one. It spins on the spot and is poor in a straight line: for fishing and short crossings. It is light enough to wear on your back.
- Paddle it with an oar.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse, and put it in a backpack slot to carry it on your back.
- Mend it with a small prepared hide.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:ba:
Birch bark on a light frame: fast, with a draft so shallow that it runs rapids which batter every other hull. Fragile, and carried over portages.
- Paddle it with an oar.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse.
- Mend it on the way with birch bark.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:cu:
Greased hide on a wooden frame: light, and it carries cargo along the coast under oars. Rocks hole the hide, and it wears unless greased with rendered fat every few days afloat. The light hull flexes with the sea and rides over swells that come aboard heavier boats.
- Paddle it with an oar.
- Pick it up with shift + rightmouse.
- Grease it with rendered fat against wear, and mend holes in the hide with a large prepared hide.
roughseas:item-handbooktext-roughseas:ou:
A narrow log hull steadied by a float: the fastest thing at sea before metal. Little cargo, clumsy in tight water, and too heavy to carry or beach. The float keeps it very steady in a sea, and its raised sides seldom ship water.
- rightmouse click the halyard cleat at the mast to raise or lower the sail.
- Mend it with planks of its wood.
guide-goingtosea-text:
Going to Sea
The sea lets you cross. It never promises to.

The sea now has weather of its own. Wind rises and falls, storms cross the water, waves break on the shore, and every vessel can be worn, swamped or broken, each in its own way. A raft that is fine on a calm lake will not cross an ocean in a gale.

Before a crossing
- Read the sky and the trees: a storm shows itself before it arrives. See Wind, Storms and Currents.
- Choose a vessel that suits the trip, and check its hull. See Vessels and Their Repair.
- Take a bowl or bucket to bail with, and some material to mend the hull. See Surf, Swamping and Bailing.
- Know where you will leave the vessel. See Mooring and Anchoring.

Dangerous oceans
The Rough Seas playstyle on the new world screen makes a world with more open ocean. The Dangerous oceans world setting, on by default, decides whether the sea can harm your vessels. With it off, wind, storms and currents still come and go, but storms, lightning, surf and swamping do no harm. Rocks, rapids, weapons and wear still damage a hull either way.
guide-weather-title: Rough Seas: Wind, Storms and Currents
guide-weather-text:
Wind
Wind has a direction and a strength, and it changes over hours. The stronger it blows and the more open the water, the higher the waves. Trees, clouds, rain and the roll of a boat all follow it, so look around before you push off.

Storms
Storms drift across the world. Squalls favour warm, wet summers and gales cool winters, and the worst form in the subtropics.
- Squalls are small and pass within hours.
- Gales cover a great area and can blow for a day or two.
- Hurricanes last for days and bring the strongest wind of all.
A storm warns you first: treetops start to sway, the sky darkens and the swell rises. That is your time to make for shore.

Lightning
Warm storms bring thunder, and lightning strikes inside them. A mast draws it, and a strike can split a hull. Cold gales bring no thunder.

Currents
The oceans turn in great slow circles. The strongest current runs along an ocean's western shore, and small seas barely move. In the middle latitudes it carries warm water and the eastern side is cool; nearer the equator and nearer the poles it turns over. A vessel left alone drifts with the current, so tie it up or anchor it before you step ashore.
guide-vessels-title: Rough Seas: Vessels and Their Repair
guide-vessels-text:
Condition
Every vessel has a hull, and the hull wears and breaks. Look at a vessel to read its condition, from sound through scratched, scarred and damaged to breaking up, and how much of the hull is left in percent. The hull shows it too: first scratches, then split wood, frayed reed, torn bark or holed hide. The condition stays with the vessel when you pick it up, as durability on the item.

What breaks a hull
- Running into rock or shore at speed. Easing in to a landing is safe.
- Rapids, which batter every hull except the bark canoe.
- Breaking surf, lightning, explosions and axes.
- Wear: a reed boat soaks through in a few days afloat, and a currach needs greasing every few days; look at it to see when.
What a hull is made of decides how much it takes: an oak raft breaks after a few hard knocks, a sailboat shrugs off far more.

Mending
Hold the vessel's own material and rightmouse click its hull to mend it, one patch at a time. Each patch is hard work and makes you hungry, and a hull with nothing to mend says so. Logs mend a wooden raft and bamboo stakes a bamboo one, planks of the same wood mend a sailboat, and each boat's handbook page says what mends it. A broken vessel is gone: only floating wreckage is left.

Choosing a vessel
- Reed boat: cheap and quick, good for one trip.
- Dugout: the toughest hull on rivers and lakes, but it rolls in a sea.
- Coracle: turns on the spot, carried on your back.
- Birch-bark canoe: fast, runs rapids, fragile.
- Hide currach: carries cargo and rides over the swell.
- Outrigger canoe: fast and steady on open sea.
- Sailboat: strong and roomy, the vessel for long voyages.
guide-surf-title: Rough Seas: Surf, Swamping and Bailing
guide-surf-text:
Surf
Where shallow water meets big waves, they break. Out at sea a high swell breaks only now and then, but close to shore in rough weather every wave becomes surf. A breaking wave strikes the hull hard, so land in calm weather or in a sheltered bay.

Shipping water
When the waves run higher than a vessel's sides, water comes aboard. Boats with a hull, from the coracle to the sailboat, hold it in their bilge: look at the vessel to see how many litres it carries, and you see the water in the boat itself. Water aboard weighs it down: it rides lower, ships more, rolls harder and gets slower.

Swamping
A full bilge swamps the vessel. It lies awash: it cannot be paddled or sat in, but you can hold on to it, bail it out, wait for a lull, or leave it. Wood floats, so a swamped boat stays afloat; only a sailboat, heavy with ballast, sinks. Rafts and reed boats hold no water, as it washes straight through them.

Capsizing
A big enough breaker overturns a small boat, throws everyone aboard into the sea and fills the bilge. The coracle goes over first, then the dugout and the birch-bark canoe, then the reed boat. The raft, the currach and the outrigger ride out far more, and the sailboat most of all.

Bailing
Hold an empty bowl, jug or bucket and keep rightmouse pressed while looking into the boat: looking at the sea, you fill the bowl from it instead. Each scoop throws water over the side. In a storm, keep bailing: an open sailboat left alone in a severe gale swamps within minutes.
guide-mooring-text:
A vessel left alone drifts with the current, and a storm can throw it onto the shore.

Tying up
Tie a vessel to a fence post ashore with a rope, the way you tie an animal. The post holds it, but a strong enough pull snaps the rope.

Anchoring
A sailboat carries a stone anchor in its prow. rightmouse click it with an empty hand to let it go or haul it up. The anchor holds best when you let out plenty of rope, about five times the depth of the water. Its own rope reaches about 120 metres. For deeper water, stow an anchor warp at the foot of the mast with ctrl + rightmouse.
- Too little rope, and the anchor drags in a storm.
- Water deeper than the rope, and the anchor hangs and holds nothing.
- A rope that snaps takes the anchor with it.
While someone steers the vessel, the anchor does not hold it but drags along behind.

Leaving a vessel
An anchored vessel takes the waves more gently, but it still ships water and can still capsize. Moored close to shore with no one nearby, it may be thrown up on the beach when a storm comes. Far from shore and well anchored, it rides out the night.
